title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
abstract: We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations.   Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.
summary: This paper introduces QuantumBilliards.jl, a comprehensive Julia library designed for high-performance computation of quantum spectra and eigenstates in 2D quantum billiards. It unifies several state-of-the-art numerical techniques, including advanced boundary integral methods and accelerated eigensolvers. This tool is crucial for studying quantum chaos and testing semiclassical conjectures in various geometries and fields.
main_problem: The core problem is solving the two-dimensional Helmholtz eigenproblem for quantum billiards, which requires finding the spectrum and eigenstates subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions.
main_result: The authors present QuantumBilliards.jl, a high-performance Julia library that unifies multiple advanced numerical techniques for solving this challenging eigenvalue problem.
method: The library implements a suite of accelerated eigensolvers, including the Vergini–Saraceno scaling method, EBIM, Beyn's contour-integral method, and CORK, alongside basis-expansion and boundary-integral formulations.
model_or_system: The model is a 2D quantum billiard defined by a bounded domain B, governed by the Helmholtz equation derived from the Schrödinger equation. The system can be generalized to include magnetic fields or hyperbolic metrics.
key_observables: Eigenvalues (energy levels $E=k^2$), eigenfunctions, Poincaré–Husimi (PH) phase-space representations, and spectral statistics (Poisson, GOE, GUE).
important_parameters: Wavenumber $k$, characteristic length $L$, and the semiclassical limit ($kL \gg 1$).
main_assumptions: The methods rely on complex mathematical machinery, such as analytic continuation, logarithmic splitting, and the assumption of convergence for various basis sets and quadrature rules.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate examples of scarred eigenstates in the stadium billiard, comparisons of spectral statistics against Wigner surmise, and visualizations of eigenstates in magnetic and hyperbolic billiards.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first establishing the quantum billiard problem, then detailing multiple numerical approaches (basis expansion, boundary integral methods), and finally showcasing the unified implementation and application of accelerated solvers to complex geometries and fields.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum chaos, the advanced numerical techniques—such as structured linearization, compact Krylov methods, and specialized boundary integral formulations—are highly relevant for simulating complex quantum systems in AMO physics or open quantum systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Examples of scarred eigenstates of the stadium billiard with half width equal to 1. The wavenumbers are k = 74.1838018, 74.22509066, 74.26339429.

Figure 2: Examples of Helmholtz basis functions implemented in QuantumBilliards.jl. Left: a real plane-wave basis function for the sta- dium billiard. Right: a corner-adapted Fourier–Bessel basis function for a triangular billiard, centered at a corner so that the boundary conditions are incorporated directly into the basis. Eigenfunctions are constructed as linear combinations of such functions according to Eq. (6). For high-accuracy calculations, additional evanescent plane waves may be required near parts of the boundary that are difficult to resolve.

Figure 3: Direct spectral sweep for the stadium billiard in the (−1,−1) reflection- symmetry sector over k ∈[20,25]. The DM, PSM, DLP, and CFIE tensions are defined differently and therefore have different absolute scales, but their minima occur at the same physical eigenwavenumbers. The corresponding eigenfunctions are shown at various sweep tension minima and illustrate the different spatial structures of states. The wavefunction color-plots are shown in the logarithmic scale, with the black lines being the nodal lines.

Figure 4: Poles of the inverse of the Fredholm matrix k as found via Beyn’s method. The 10 low-lying states were obtained with a single solve call. The blue points show the residual τ(k) = ||A(k)v(k)||
Figure 5: Type diagram of the solver types in the library. Abstract types are shown in blue and concrete types in yellow. The arrows connect each super-type to its subtypes.
